name: The Roof Out of Scale With Its House

severity_by_style.why: Uniformity of exposure across wall and roof is a hard rule of the style, not a refinement.
Graduated coursing is the type's whole roof logic.
Within the 5-7 in band the difference is a refinement that separates good from very good.
The type has no traditional coursing claim.

symptom: The roof's course lines are the wrong size for the building they are on: sixteen-inch 'shakes' at a ten-inch exposure on a small cottage, or a five-inch slate exposure on a sixty-foot front, so the roof reads either coarse and under-coursed or fine and busy. The related failure is a ridge, hip or valley detail of a completely different visual weight from the field - a hip cap twice the thickness of a field course.

cause.explanation: Exposure is set by the material's warranty schedule and by labour, not by the building. Every extra inch of exposure removes courses and therefore removes both material and time: going from a 5 in to a 7 1/2 in exposure on a wood shingle roof removes a third of the shingles and a third of the nailing. The estimator picks the maximum exposure the warranty allows, which is a number about the material and contains no information about the house.
cause.cost_saved: 20-35 per cent of the roof's material and labour between the tight and the loose end of a material's permitted exposure range.

rule_violated.statement: Shingle length 18-24 in, exposure 5-7 in and not more than one third of the length, width 3-8 in, butt 3/8-3/4 in, side gap 1/8-1/2 in, course stagger not less than 1.5 in (NPS Preservation Brief 19).

The number of courses between eave and ridge is one of the few things that tells the eye how big a roof is. A roof whose courses cannot be counted at fifty feet has no texture and reads as a coloured plane.

correct_practice: Read the coursing against the building, not only against the warranty. Wood shingle: 18-24 in long at 5-7 in exposure, never more than one third of the shingle's length, in 3-8 in widths with a minimum 1.5 in stagger between courses. Slate: an 18 x 10 in slate with a 3 in head lap gives a 7.5 in exposure, and smaller slates at tighter courses belong on smaller and steeper roofs - which is why a good slate roof on a cottage is not simply a scaled-down version of one on a mansion. The scale rule: a modest house should show enough courses to read as a texture, roughly 25 to 40 from eave to ridge, while a large house can take larger units and fewer, coarser courses. And the material's units must remain legible as units at the distance from which the building is normally seen.

fixes.right: Specify the exposure as a dimension on the drawing, chosen from the roof's slope length and the building's size, rather than leaving it to the estimator.
fixes.cheap: Reduce the exposure by an inch. On slate and wood it costs material in proportion, but on a small roof the absolute number is small and it is the difference between a roof with texture and a roof without. And it is free to get the ridge and hip right: specify that hip and ridge units may not exceed twice a field course's exposure.
fixes.dishonest: Using an oversized 'designer' shingle to make a small roof look grander. Coarse coursing on a small roof makes the house look smaller, not larger, because the courses are the only unit of measurement the eye has.

test.note: Directly countable in a photograph of a whole roof plane. A modest house should show enough courses to read as a texture; a great house takes larger units and fewer, coarser courses. A roof whose courses cannot be counted at fifty feet has no texture and reads as a coloured plane.

secondary_tests.note: Not more than one third of the shingle's length to the weather - the NPS Brief 19 rule, which is simultaneously the watertightness rule and the scale rule, and the reason the two cannot be traded against each other.
A cap more than about twice a field course reads as a different material. This half of the test is free to get right and is almost always got wrong.
Mixing within one plane - two coursings, or a metal accent panel inserted into a shingled slope - announces that the roof is a collection rather than a surface.

detection: Count courses from eave to ridge in a photograph and divide by the roof's slope length in feet. Wood shingle at a 6 in exposure gives two courses to the foot; slate at 7.5 in gives 1.6; a standing-seam panel gives none, and its ribs give a vertical rhythm instead at 12-20 in. Then compare the ridge and hip detail's apparent thickness against a field course: a cap more than about twice a field course reads as a different material. Finally, look for mixing within one plane - two coursings, or a metal accent panel inserted into a shingled slope, both of which announce that the roof is a collection rather than a surface.

exceptions.why: A 4-6 in exposure held uniform across the ENTIRE building, wall and roof alike, is definitional - deliberately fine and deliberately monotonous, so that the two surfaces read as one skin.
exceptions.bounds: The fineness is only correct if the wall shingles match it exactly. A fine roof over a coarse wall is the fault in a different place.

bounds_test.note: The fineness is only correct if the wall shingles match it exactly. A fine roof over a coarse wall is the fault in a different place.

exceptions.why: Heavy shakes at a large exposure are correct on a bungalow, because the whole material palette is deliberately coarse - clinker brick, boulder, heavy timber - and the roof is part of that argument.
exceptions.bounds: The coarseness must be consistent with the rest of the palette. A heavy shake roof over smooth machine-lap siding and vinyl windows is not this.

bounds_test.note: The coarseness must be consistent with the rest of the palette - clinker brick, boulder, heavy timber. A heavy shake roof over smooth machine-lap siding and vinyl windows is not this.

exceptions.why: Barrel tile's scale is set by the tile at 15-18 in, and the roof is meant to read coarse against a smooth plastered wall.
exceptions.bounds: The contrast with the smooth wall is what makes it work; a coarse tile over a coarse wall loses the argument.

bounds_test.note: The contrast with the smooth plastered wall is what makes it work; a coarse tile over a coarse wall loses the argument.

exceptions.why: Stone slates are graduated deliberately - large at the eave, small at the ridge - so a single exposure figure does not describe the roof at all.
exceptions.bounds: The graduation must be continuous and the courses must diminish monotonically; random sizes are not graduation.

bounds_test.note: The graduation must be continuous and the courses must diminish monotonically; random sizes are not graduation.

inverted_by.statement: Varying exposure is the fault. 4-6 in held uniform across the ENTIRE building, wall and roof alike, is definitional - deliberately fine and deliberately monotonous, so the two surfaces read as one skin.
A uniform exposure is the fault. Stone slates are graduated - large at the eave, small at the ridge - so a single exposure figure does not describe the roof at all.

confused_with.difference: That is a material imitating another. This is a real material at the wrong grain for its building.
The ridge half of this fault overlaps, but that one is specifically about ventilation driving a foreign ridge material.
